(1826), orth. var.}} |synonyms_ref = }} '''''Wisteria''''' is a {{ill|Genus|en|Genus|WD=Q34740|lt=Genus|1=Genus}} of {{ill|Flowering plant|en|Flowering plant|WD=Q25314|lt=Flowering plant|1=Flowering plant}}s in the {{ill|legume|en|legume|WD=Q145909|lt=legume|1=Legume}} family, {{ill|Fabaceae|en|Fabaceae|WD=Q44448|lt=Fabaceae|1=Fabaceae}} (Leguminosae). The genus includes four species of woody twining vines that are native to {{ill|China|en|China|WD=Q148|lt=China|1=China}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}, {{ill|Korea|en|Korea|WD=Q18097|lt=Korea|1=Korea}}, {{ill|Vietnam|en|Vietnam|WD=Q881|lt=Vietnam|1=Vietnam}}, southern {{ill|Canada|en|Canada|WD=Q16|lt=Canada|1=Canada}}, the {{ill|Eastern United States|en|Eastern United States|WD=Q1189650|lt=Eastern United States|1=Eastern United States}}, and north of {{ill|Iran|en|Iran|WD=Q794|lt=Iran|1=Iran}}. They were later introduced to France, Germany and various other countries in Europe. Some species are popular ornamental plants. The genus name is also used as the English name, and may then be spelt 'wistaria'. In some countries in Western and Central Europe, ''Wisteria'' is also known by a variant spelling of the {{ill|Genus|en|Genus|WD=Q34740|lt=Genus|1=Genus}} in which species were formerly placed, ''{{ill|Glycine (plant)|en|Glycine (plant)|WD=Q311395|lt=Glycine|1=Glycine (plant)}}''. Examples include the French ''glycines'', the German ''Glyzinie'', and the Polish ''glicynia''. The aquatic flowering plant commonly called wisteria or 'water wisteria' is ''{{ill|Hygrophila difformis|en|Hygrophila difformis|WD=Q1431832|lt=Hygrophila difformis|1=Hygrophila difformis}}'', in the family {{ill|Acanthaceae|en|Acanthaceae|WD=Q53475|lt=Acanthaceae|1=Acanthaceae}}. ==Description== [[File:Wisteria floribunda MHNT.BOT.2008.1.38.jpg|right|thumb|Seeds and seedpods of ''{{ill|Wisteria floribunda|en|Wisteria floribunda|WD=Q1329209|lt=Wisteria floribunda|1=Wisteria floribunda}}'' (Japanese wisteria). The seeds of all ''Wisteria'' species contain high levels of the [[:en:wisterin|wisterin]] toxin and are especially poisonous.]] Wisterias climb by twining their {{ill|Plant stem|en|Plant stem|WD=Q134267|lt=stem|1=Plant stem}}s around any available support. ''{{ill|Wisteria floribunda|en|Wisteria floribunda|WD=Q1329209|lt=W. floribunda|1=Wisteria floribunda}}'' (Japanese wisteria) twines clockwise when viewed from above, while ''{{ill|Wisteria sinensis|en|Wisteria sinensis|WD=Q159116|lt=W. sinensis|1=Wisteria sinensis}}'' (Chinese wisteria) twines counterclockwise. This is an aid in identifying the two most common species of wisteria. They can climb as high as {{convert|20|m|ft|abbr=on}} above the ground and spread out {{convert|10|m|ft|abbr=on}} laterally. The world's largest known wisteria is the [[:en:Sierra Madre Wisteria|Sierra Madre Wisteria]] in {{ill|Sierra Madre, California|en|Sierra Madre, California|WD=Q174026|lt=Sierra Madre, California|1=Sierra Madre, California}}, measuring more than {{convert|1|acre|ha}} in size and weighing 250 tons. Planted in 1894, it is of the 'Chinese lavender' variety. The {{ill|Leaf|en|Leaf|WD=Q33971|lt=leaves|1=Leaf}} are alternate, 15 to 35 cm long, {{ill|Pinnation|en|Pinnation|WD=Q3756157|lt=pinnate|1=Pinnation}}, with 9 to 19 leaflets. The {{ill|Flower|en|Flower|WD=Q506|lt=Flower|1=Flower}}s have drooping {{ill|raceme|en|raceme|WD=Q158583|lt=raceme|1=Raceme}}s that vary in length from species to species. ''{{ill|Wisteria frutescens|en|Wisteria frutescens|WD=Q8027753|lt=W. frutescens|1=Wisteria frutescens}}'' (American wisteria) has the shortest racemes, {{convert|5|–|7|cm}}. ''W. floribunda'' (Japanese wisteria) has the longest racemes, {{convert|90|cm}} in some {{ill|Variety (botany)|en|Variety (botany)|WD=Q767728|lt=varieties|1=Variety (botany)}} and {{convert|120|cm}} or {{convert|200|cm}} in some [[:en:cultivars|cultivars]]. The flowers come in a variety of colors, including white, lilac, purple, and pink, and some ''{{ill|Wisteria brachybotrys|en|Wisteria brachybotrys|WD=Q5783537|lt=W. brachybotrys|1=Wisteria brachybotrys}}'' (Silky wisteria) and ''W. floribunda'' cultivars have particularly remarkable colors. The flowers are fragrant, and especially cultivars of ''W. brachybotrys'', ''W. floribunda'', and ''W. sinensis'' are noted for their sweet and musky scents. Flowering is in spring (just before or as the leaves open) in some Asian species, and in mid to late summer in the American species. ==Taxonomy== {{See also|Wisterieae#Taxonomy}} The genus ''Wisteria'' was established by {{ill|Thomas Nuttall|en|Thomas Nuttall|WD=Q728337|lt=Thomas Nuttall|1=Thomas Nuttall}} in 1818. He based the genus on ''{{ill|Wisteria frutescens|en|Wisteria frutescens|WD=Q8027753|lt=Wisteria frutescens|1=Wisteria frutescens}}'', previously included in the genus ''{{ill|Glycine (plant)|en|Glycine (plant)|WD=Q311395|lt=Glycine|1=Glycine (plant)}}''. Nuttall stated that he named the genus in memory of the American physician and anatomist {{ill|Caspar Wistar (physician)|en|Caspar Wistar (physician)|WD=Q347595|lt=Caspar Wistar|1=Caspar Wistar (physician)}} (1761–1818). Both men were living in Philadelphia at the time, where Wistar was a professor in the [[:en:Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania|School of Medicine]] at the {{ill|University of Pennsylvania|en|University of Pennsylvania|WD=Q49117|lt=University of Pennsylvania|1=University of Pennsylvania}}. Questioned about the spelling later, Nuttall said it was for "[[:en:euphony|euphony]]", but his biographer speculated that it may have something to do with Nuttall's friend Charles Jones Wister Sr., of {{ill|Grumblethorpe|en|Grumblethorpe|WD=Q5612044|lt=Grumblethorpe|1=Grumblethorpe}}, the grandson of the merchant [[John Wister]]. Various sources assert that the naming occurred in {{ill|Philadelphia|en|Philadelphia|WD=Q1345|lt=Philadelphia|1=Philadelphia}}. It has been suggested that the Portuguese botanist and geologist {{ill|José Correia da Serra|en|José Correia da Serra|WD=Q2656605|lt=José Francisco Corrêa da Serra|1=José Correia da Serra}}, who lived in Philadelphia beginning in 1812, four years before his appointment as ambassador of {{ill|Portugal|en|Portugal|WD=Q45|lt=Portugal|1=Portugal}} to the United States, and a friend of Wistar, proposed the name "Wistaria" in his obituary of Wistar. As the spelling is apparently deliberate, there is no justification for changing the genus name under the {{ill|International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants|en|International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants|WD=Q693148|lt=International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants|1=International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants}}. ===Classification=== The genus was previously placed in the tribe {{ill|Millettieae|en|Millettieae|WD=Q141908|lt=Millettieae|1=Millettieae}}. {{ill|Molecular phylogenetics|en|Molecular phylogenetics|WD=Q2007033|lt=Molecular phylogenetic|1=Molecular phylogenetics}} studies from 2000 onwards showed that ''Wisteria'', along with other genera such as ''{{ill|Callerya|en|Callerya|WD=Q2705210|lt=Callerya|1=Callerya}}'' and ''{{ill|Afgekia|en|Afgekia|WD=Q3310234|lt=Afgekia|1=Afgekia}}'', were related and quite distinct from other members of the Millettieae. A more detailed study in 2019 reached the same conclusion, and moved ''Wisteria'' to the expanded tribe {{ill|Wisterieae|en|Wisterieae|WD=Q92314202|lt=Wisterieae|1=Wisterieae}}. ===Species=== [[File:足利の藤 (Wisteria trellises in Ashikaga) 29 Apr, 2009 - panoramio.jpg|thumb|250x250px|''W. floribunda'' at [[Ashikaga Flower Park]] ([[:ja:あしかがフラワーパーク|ja]]) in {{lang|ja-Latn|{{ill|Ashikaga, Tochigi|en|Ashikaga, Tochigi|WD=Q374477|lt=Ashikaga, Tochigi|1=Ashikaga, Tochigi}}|italic=no}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}. ''Wisteria macrostachys'') || American wisteria || United States (Kentucky to Texas, to Florida, as well as Iowa, Michigan, and New York) |- |[[File:Wisteria sinensis 5Dsr 0101.jpg|120px]] ||''{{ill|Wisteria sinensis|en|Wisteria sinensis|WD=Q159116|lt=Wisteria sinensis|1=Wisteria sinensis}}'' ({{ill|John Sims (taxonomist)|en|John Sims (taxonomist)|WD=Q2430593|lt=Sims|1=John Sims (taxonomist)}}) DC. || Chinese wisteria || China (Guangxi, Guizhou, Hebei, Henan, Hubei, Shaanxi, and Yunnan.) |} {{Clear}} ==Ecology== {{Unreferenced section|date=May 2024}} ''Wisteria'' species are used as food by the {{ill|larva|en|larva|WD=Q129270|lt=larva|1=Larva}}e of some {{ill|Lepidoptera|en|Lepidoptera|WD=Q28319|lt=Lepidoptera|1=Lepidoptera}} species including the {{ill|brown-tail moth|en|brown-tail moth|WD=Q45902|lt=brown-tail moth|1=Brown-tail moth}}. ==Toxicity== The {{ill|Seed|en|Seed|WD=Q40763|lt=Seed|1=Seed}}s are produced in pods similar to those of ''Laburnum'', and, like the seeds of that genus, are {{ill|poison|en|poison|WD=Q40867|lt=poison|1=Poison}}ous. All parts of the plant contain a {{ill|saponin|en|saponin|WD=Q207653|lt=saponin|1=Saponin}} called wisterin, which is {{ill|Toxicity|en|Toxicity|WD=Q274160|lt=toxic|1=Toxicity}} if ingested, and may cause {{ill|dizziness|en|dizziness|WD=Q10916362|lt=dizziness|1=Dizziness}}, confusion, speech problems, nausea, {{ill|Vomiting|en|Vomiting|WD=Q127076|lt=Vomiting|1=Vomiting}}, stomach pains, {{ill|Diarrhea|en|Diarrhea|WD=Q40878|lt=Diarrhea|1=Diarrhea}} and collapse. There is debate over whether the concentration outside of the seeds is sufficient to cause poisoning. Wisteria seeds have caused poisoning in children and pets of many countries, producing mild to severe gastroenteritis and other effects. ==Cultivation== {{multiple image |align=right |direction=horizontal |header_align=center |header= |image1=Wisteria at Nymans Gardens, West Sussex, England May 2006.JPG |width1=200 |alt1= |caption1=Wisteria at {{ill|Nymans|en|Nymans|WD=Q7071172|lt=Nymans|1=Nymans}} Gardens
({{ill|West Sussex|en|West Sussex|WD=Q23287|lt=West Sussex|1=West Sussex}}, England) |image2=Climbing_wisteria_(Stresa,_Italy).jpg |width2=200 |alt2= |caption2=Trunk of mature wisteria supported by balustrade ({{ill|Stresa|en|Stresa|WD=Q23700|lt=Stresa|1=Stresa}}, Italy) }} In North America, ''{{ill|Wisteria floribunda|en|Wisteria floribunda|WD=Q1329209|lt=W. floribunda|1=Wisteria floribunda}}'' (Japanese wisteria) and ''{{ill|Wisteria sinensis|en|Wisteria sinensis|WD=Q159116|lt=W. sinensis|1=Wisteria sinensis}}'' (Chinese wisteria) are far more popular than other species for their abundance of flowers, clusters of large flowers, variety of flower colors, and fragrance. ''W. sinensis'' was brought to the United States for horticultural purposes in 1816, while ''W. floribunda'' was introduced around 1830. Because of their hardiness and tendency to {{ill|escaped plant|en|escaped plant|WD=Q1494641|lt=escape cultivation|1=Escaped plant}}, these non-native wisterias are considered {{ill|Invasive species|en|Invasive species|WD=Q183368|lt=Invasive species|1=Invasive species}} in many parts of the {{ill|United States|en|United States|WD=Q30|lt=U.S.|1=United States}}, especially the {{ill|Southeastern United States|en|Southeastern United States|WD=Q1139046|lt=Southeast|1=Southeastern United States}}, due to their ability to overtake and choke out other native plant species. ''{{ill|Wisteria floribunda|en|Wisteria floribunda|WD=Q1329209|lt=W. floribunda|1=Wisteria floribunda}}'' (Japanese wisteria), which has the longest racemes of wisteria species, is decorative and has given rise to many {{ill|Cultivar|en|Cultivar|WD=Q4886|lt=Cultivar|1=Cultivar}}s that have won the prestigious {{ill|Award of Garden Merit|en|Award of Garden Merit|WD=Q3501416|lt=Award of Garden Merit|1=Award of Garden Merit}}. Wisteria, especially ''{{ill|Wisteria sinensis|en|Wisteria sinensis|WD=Q159116|lt=W. sinensis|1=Wisteria sinensis}}'' (Chinese wisteria), is very hardy and fast-growing. It can grow in fairly poor-quality soils, but prefers fertile, moist, well-drained soil. It thrives in full sun. It can be propagated via hardwood cutting, softwood cuttings, or seed. However, specimens grown from seed can take decades to bloom; for this reason, gardeners usually grow plants that have been started from rooted cuttings or grafted {{ill|Cultivar|en|Cultivar|WD=Q4886|lt=Cultivar|1=Cultivar}}s known to flower well. Another reason for failure to bloom can be excessive fertilizer (particularly {{ill|nitrogen|en|nitrogen|WD=Q627|lt=nitrogen|1=Nitrogen}}). Wisteria has nitrogen fixing capability (provided by ''{{ill|Rhizobia|en|Rhizobia|WD=Q9164450|lt=Rhizobia|1=Rhizobia}}'' bacteria in root nodules), and thus mature plants may benefit from added {{ill|potassium|en|potassium|WD=Q703|lt=potassium|1=Potassium}} and {{ill|phosphate|en|phosphate|WD=Q46220103|lt=phosphate|1=Phosphate}}, but not nitrogen. Finally, wisteria can be reluctant to bloom before it has reached maturity. Maturation may require only a few years, as in ''{{ill|Wisteria macrostachya|en|Wisteria macrostachya|WD=Q8027752|lt=W. macrostachya|1=Wisteria macrostachya}}'' (Kentucky wisteria), or nearly twenty, as in ''W. sinensis''. Maturation can be forced by physically abusing the main {{ill|Trunk (botany)|en|Trunk (botany)|WD=Q193472|lt=trunk|1=Trunk (botany)}}, root pruning, or {{ill|Drought|en|Drought|WD=Q43059|lt=Drought|1=Drought}} stress. Wisteria can grow into a mound when unsupported, but is at its best when allowed to clamber up a tree, {{ill|pergola|en|pergola|WD=Q264458|lt=pergola|1=Pergola}}, wall, or other supporting structure. ''W. floribunda'' (Japanese wisteria) with longer racemes is the best choice to grow along a pergola. ''W. sinensis'' (Chinese wisteria) with shorter racemes is the best choice for growing along a wall. Whatever the case, the support must be very sturdy, because mature wisteria can become immensely strong with heavy wrist-thick {{ill|Trunk (botany)|en|Trunk (botany)|WD=Q193472|lt=trunk|1=Trunk (botany)}}s and {{ill|Plant stem|en|Plant stem|WD=Q134267|lt=stem|1=Plant stem}}s. These can collapse latticework, crush thin wooden posts, and even strangle large trees. Wisteria allowed to grow on houses can cause damage to gutters, downspouts, and similar structures. Wisteria flowers develop in buds near the base of the previous year's growth, so {{ill|pruning|en|pruning|WD=Q500094|lt=pruning|1=Pruning}} back side shoots to the basal few buds in early spring can enhance the visibility of the flowers. If it is desired to control the size of the plant, the side shoots can be shortened to between 20 and 40 cm long in midsummer, and back to {{convert|10|to|20|cm}} in the fall. Once the plant is a few years old, a relatively compact, free-flowering form can be achieved by pruning off the new tendrils three times during the growing season in the summer months. The flowers of some varieties are edible, and can even be used to make wine. Others are said to be toxic. Careful identification by an expert is strongly recommended before consuming this or any wild plant. In the United Kingdom, the national collection of wisteria is held by Chris Lane at the Witch Hazel Nursery in {{ill|Newington, Swale|en|Newington, Swale|WD=Q10748183|lt=Newington|1=Newington, Swale}}, near {{ill|Sittingbourne|en|Sittingbourne|WD=Q1626044|lt=Sittingbourne|1=Sittingbourne}} in {{ill|Kent|en|Kent|WD=Q23298|lt=Kent|1=Kent}}. {{Clear}} ==Art and symbolism== [[File:Sagari Fuji (No background and Black color drawing).svg|thumb|right|150px|{{transliteration|ja|Sagari fuji mon}} (Wisteria {{transliteration|ja|[[Mon (emblem)|mon]]}})]] Wisteria and their racemes have been widely used in Japan throughout the centuries and were a popular symbol in {{nihongo3|family crests||[[Mon (emblem)|mon]]}} and heraldry. Wisteria is one of the five most commonly used motifs in the {{transliteration|ja|mon}}, and there are more than 150 types of wisteria {{transliteration|ja|mon}}. Because of its longevity and fertility, wisteria was considered an auspicious plant and was favored as a {{transliteration|ja|mon}}, and was adopted and popularized by the [[Fujiwara clan]] as their {{transliteration|ja|mon}}.{{cite web|url=https://www.nippon.com/en/japan-data/h01578/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230420034414/https://www.nippon.com/en/japan-data/h01578/|title="Kamon": Japan's Family Crests|publisher=nippon.com|date=10 February 2023|archive-date=20 April 2023|access-date=29 April 2023}}{{cite web|url=https://irohakamon.com/kamon/fuji/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230212111436/https://irohakamon.com/kamon/fuji/|script-title=ja:藤紋（ふじ）について|language=ja|publisher=Kamon no iroha|archive-date=12 February 2023|access-date=29 April 2023}} {{multiple image |direction=horizontal |width1=147 |width2=150 |align=left |footer=Left to right: ''View of Oyster Bay'' (1908), by [[:en:Louis C. Tiffany|Louis C. Tiffany]], with wisteria evoking the estate of its patrons, {{ill|Wistariahurst|en|Wistariahurst|WD=Q8027742|lt=Wistariahurst|1=Wistariahurst}}; ''Japanese wisteria and white-bellied green pigeons'' (1883), a woodblock print by {{ill|Kōno Bairei|en|Kōno Bairei|WD=Q3201302|lt=Kōno Bairei|1=Kōno Bairei}} |image1=At the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York 2017 04 - View of Oyster Bay. New York City.jpg |image2=Bairei kachō gafu, Spring 12, Japanese wisteria and white-bellied green pigeons.jpg}} One popular dance in {{ill|Kabuki|en|Kabuki|WD=Q199701|lt=Kabuki|1=Kabuki}} known as the ''{{ill|Fuji Musume|en|Fuji Musume|WD=Q11623783|lt=Fuji Musume|1=Fuji Musume}}'' (or 'The Wisteria Maiden'), is the sole extant dance of a series of five personifying dances in which a maiden becomes the embodiment of the spirit of wisteria. In the West, both in building materials such as tile, as well as stained glass, wisterias have been used both in realism and stylistically in artistic works and industrial design. {{Clear}} ==References== {{Reflist|refs= {{cite book |last=Baird |first=Merrily C. |year=2001 |title=Symbols of Japan: Thematic Motifs in Art and Design |publisher=Random House, Inc. |location=New York |page=67 |oclc=237418692}} {{cite book |last=Bryson |first=Bill |author-link=Bill Bryson |title=A Short History of Nearly Everything |edition=1st |year=2003 |publisher=Broadway Books |location=New York, NY |isbn=0-375-43200-0 |chapter=Ch. 6 — Science Red in Tooth and Claw |url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780375432002}} {{cite web |last=Charters |first=Michael L. |work=California Plant Names: Latin and Greek Meanings and Derivations |title=Page W |url=http://www.calflora.net/botanicalnames/pageW.html |access-date=2011-05-15}} {{Cite journal |last1=Compton |first1=James A. |last2=Schrire |first2=Brian D. |last3=Könyves |first3=Kálmán |last4=Forest |first4=Félix |last5=Malakasi |first5=Panagiota |last6=Sawai Mattapha |last7=Sirichamorn |first7=Yotsawate |date=2019 |title=The ''Callerya'' Group redefined and Tribe Wisterieae (Fabaceae) emended based on morphology and data from nuclear and chloroplast DNA sequences |journal=PhytoKeys |issue=125 |pages=1–112 |doi=10.3897/phytokeys.125.34877 |pmid=31303810 |pmc=6610001 |name-list-style=amp |doi-access=free }} {{cite book |last1=Cotter |first1=John L. |last2=Roberts |first2=Daniel G. |last3=Parrington |first3=Michael |year=1994 |title=The Buried Past: An Archaeological History of Philadelphia |publication-place=Philadelphia |publisher=University of Pennsylvania Press |page=339 |name-list-style=amp}} {{Cite web |date=15 April 2014 |title=Canadian Poisonous Plants Information System - needed|date=June 2024}}{{Automatic taxobox |image = Chinese Wisteria Blütentrauben.JPG |image_caption = Flowering ''{{ill|Wisteria sinensis|en|Wisteria sinensis|WD=Q159116|lt=Wisteria sinensis|1=Wisteria sinensis}}'' |taxon = Wisteria |authority = {{ill|Thomas Nuttall|en|Thomas Nuttall|WD=Q728337|lt=Nutt.|1=Thomas Nuttall}} (1818), nom. cons. |synonyms = * ''Bradburia'' {{small|Spreng. (1826)}} * ''Diplonyx'' Raf. (1817), nom. rej. * ''Kraunhia'' Raf. (1891), nom. superfl. * ''Phaseoloides'' Duhamel (1755), nom. rej. * ''Rehsonia'' Stritch (1984) * ''Thyrsanthus'' {{small|Elliott (1818), nom. illeg.}} * ''Wistaria'' {{small|Nutt. ex Spreng. (1826), orth. var.}} |synonyms_ref = }} '''''Wisteria''''' is a {{ill|Genus|en|Genus|WD=Q34740|lt=Genus|1=Genus}} of {{ill|Flowering plant|en|Flowering plant|WD=Q25314|lt=Flowering plant|1=Flowering plant}}s in the {{ill|legume|en|legume|WD=Q145909|lt=legume|1=Legume}} family, {{ill|Fabaceae|en|Fabaceae|WD=Q44448|lt=Fabaceae|1=Fabaceae}} (Leguminosae). The genus includes four species of woody twining vines that are native to {{ill|China|en|China|WD=Q148|lt=China|1=China}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}, {{ill|Korea|en|Korea|WD=Q18097|lt=Korea|1=Korea}}, {{ill|Vietnam|en|Vietnam|WD=Q881|lt=Vietnam|1=Vietnam}}, southern {{ill|Canada|en|Canada|WD=Q16|lt=Canada|1=Canada}}, the {{ill|Eastern United States|en|Eastern United States|WD=Q1189650|lt=Eastern United States|1=Eastern United States}}, and north of {{ill|Iran|en|Iran|WD=Q794|lt=Iran|1=Iran}}. They were later introduced to France, Germany and various other countries in Europe. Some species are popular ornamental plants. The genus name is also used as the English name, and may then be spelt 'wistaria'. In some countries in Western and Central Europe, ''Wisteria'' is also known by a variant spelling of the {{ill|Genus|en|Genus|WD=Q34740|lt=Genus|1=Genus}} in which species were formerly placed, ''{{ill|Glycine (plant)|en|Glycine (plant)|WD=Q311395|lt=Glycine|1=Glycine (plant)}}''. Examples include the French ''glycines'', the German ''Glyzinie'', and the Polish ''glicynia''. The aquatic flowering plant commonly called wisteria or 'water wisteria' is ''{{ill|Hygrophila difformis|en|Hygrophila difformis|WD=Q1431832|lt=Hygrophila difformis|1=Hygrophila difformis}}'', in the family {{ill|Acanthaceae|en|Acanthaceae|WD=Q53475|lt=Acanthaceae|1=Acanthaceae}}. ==Description== [[File:Wisteria floribunda MHNT.BOT.2008.1.38.jpg|right|thumb|Seeds and seedpods of ''{{ill|Wisteria floribunda|en|Wisteria floribunda|WD=Q1329209|lt=Wisteria floribunda|1=Wisteria floribunda}}'' (Japanese wisteria). The seeds of all ''Wisteria'' species contain high levels of the [[:en:wisterin|wisterin]] toxin and are especially poisonous.]] Wisterias climb by twining their {{ill|Plant stem|en|Plant stem|WD=Q134267|lt=stem|1=Plant stem}}s around any available support. ''{{ill|Wisteria floribunda|en|Wisteria floribunda|WD=Q1329209|lt=W. floribunda|1=Wisteria floribunda}}'' (Japanese wisteria) twines clockwise when viewed from above, while ''{{ill|Wisteria sinensis|en|Wisteria sinensis|WD=Q159116|lt=W. sinensis|1=Wisteria sinensis}}'' (Chinese wisteria) twines counterclockwise. This is an aid in identifying the two most common species of wisteria. They can climb as high as {{convert|20|m|ft|abbr=on}} above the ground and spread out {{convert|10|m|ft|abbr=on}} laterally. The world's largest known wisteria is the [[:en:Sierra Madre Wisteria|Sierra Madre Wisteria]] in {{ill|Sierra Madre, California|en|Sierra Madre, California|WD=Q174026|lt=Sierra Madre, California|1=Sierra Madre, California}}, measuring more than {{convert|1|acre|ha}} in size and weighing 250 tons. Planted in 1894, it is of the 'Chinese lavender' variety. The {{ill|Leaf|en|Leaf|WD=Q33971|lt=leaves|1=Leaf}} are alternate, 15 to 35 cm long, {{ill|Pinnation|en|Pinnation|WD=Q3756157|lt=pinnate|1=Pinnation}}, with 9 to 19 leaflets. The {{ill|Flower|en|Flower|WD=Q506|lt=Flower|1=Flower}}s have drooping {{ill|raceme|en|raceme|WD=Q158583|lt=raceme|1=Raceme}}s that vary in length from species to species. ''{{ill|Wisteria frutescens|en|Wisteria frutescens|WD=Q8027753|lt=W. frutescens|1=Wisteria frutescens}}'' (American wisteria) has the shortest racemes, {{convert|5|–|7|cm}}. ''W. floribunda'' (Japanese wisteria) has the longest racemes, {{convert|90|cm}} in some {{ill|Variety (botany)|en|Variety (botany)|WD=Q767728|lt=varieties|1=Variety (botany)}} and {{convert|120|cm}} or {{convert|200|cm}} in some [[:en:cultivars|cultivars]]. The flowers come in a variety of colors, including white, lilac, purple, and pink, and some ''{{ill|Wisteria brachybotrys|en|Wisteria brachybotrys|WD=Q5783537|lt=W. brachybotrys|1=Wisteria brachybotrys}}'' (Silky wisteria) and ''W. floribunda'' cultivars have particularly remarkable colors. The flowers are fragrant, and especially cultivars of ''W. brachybotrys'', ''W. floribunda'', and ''W. sinensis'' are noted for their sweet and musky scents. Flowering is in spring (just before or as the leaves open) in some Asian species, and in mid to late summer in the American species. ==Taxonomy== {{See also|Wisterieae#Taxonomy}} The genus ''Wisteria'' was established by {{ill|Thomas Nuttall|en|Thomas Nuttall|WD=Q728337|lt=Thomas Nuttall|1=Thomas Nuttall}} in 1818. He based the genus on ''{{ill|Wisteria frutescens|en|Wisteria frutescens|WD=Q8027753|lt=Wisteria frutescens|1=Wisteria frutescens}}'', previously included in the genus ''{{ill|Glycine (plant)|en|Glycine (plant)|WD=Q311395|lt=Glycine|1=Glycine (plant)}}''. Nuttall stated that he named the genus in memory of the American physician and anatomist {{ill|Caspar Wistar (physician)|en|Caspar Wistar (physician)|WD=Q347595|lt=Caspar Wistar|1=Caspar Wistar (physician)}} (1761–1818). Both men were living in Philadelphia at the time, where Wistar was a professor in the [[:en:Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania|School of Medicine]] at the {{ill|University of Pennsylvania|en|University of Pennsylvania|WD=Q49117|lt=University of Pennsylvania|1=University of Pennsylvania}}. Questioned about the spelling later, Nuttall said it was for "[[:en:euphony|euphony]]", but his biographer speculated that it may have something to do with Nuttall's friend Charles Jones Wister Sr., of {{ill|Grumblethorpe|en|Grumblethorpe|WD=Q5612044|lt=Grumblethorpe|1=Grumblethorpe}}, the grandson of the merchant [[John Wister]]. Various sources assert that the naming occurred in {{ill|Philadelphia|en|Philadelphia|WD=Q1345|lt=Philadelphia|1=Philadelphia}}. It has been suggested that the Portuguese botanist and geologist {{ill|José Correia da Serra|en|José Correia da Serra|WD=Q2656605|lt=José Francisco Corrêa da Serra|1=José Correia da Serra}}, who lived in Philadelphia beginning in 1812, four years before his appointment as ambassador of {{ill|Portugal|en|Portugal|WD=Q45|lt=Portugal|1=Portugal}} to the United States, and a friend of Wistar, proposed the name "Wistaria" in his obituary of Wistar. As the spelling is apparently deliberate, there is no justification for changing the genus name under the {{ill|International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants|en|International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants|WD=Q693148|lt=International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants|1=International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants}}. ===Classification=== The genus was previously placed in the tribe {{ill|Millettieae|en|Millettieae|WD=Q141908|lt=Millettieae|1=Millettieae}}. {{ill|Molecular phylogenetics|en|Molecular phylogenetics|WD=Q2007033|lt=Molecular phylogenetic|1=Molecular phylogenetics}} studies from 2000 onwards showed that ''Wisteria'', along with other genera such as ''{{ill|Callerya|en|Callerya|WD=Q2705210|lt=Callerya|1=Callerya}}'' and ''{{ill|Afgekia|en|Afgekia|WD=Q3310234|lt=Afgekia|1=Afgekia}}'', were related and quite distinct from other members of the Millettieae. A more detailed study in 2019 reached the same conclusion, and moved ''Wisteria'' to the expanded tribe {{ill|Wisterieae|en|Wisterieae|WD=Q92314202|lt=Wisterieae|1=Wisterieae}}. ===Species=== [[File:足利の藤 (Wisteria trellises in Ashikaga) 29 Apr, 2009 - panoramio.jpg|thumb|250x250px|''W. floribunda'' at [[Ashikaga Flower Park]] ([[:ja:あしかがフラワーパーク|ja]]) in {{lang|ja-Latn|{{ill|Ashikaga, Tochigi|en|Ashikaga, Tochigi|WD=Q374477|lt=Ashikaga, Tochigi|1=Ashikaga, Tochigi}}|italic=no}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}. The largest wisteria in Japan, it is dated to {{circa|1870}} and covered approximately {{convert|1,990|sqm}} {{as of|May 2008|lc=true}}.|alt=]] {{As of|2023|September}}, {{ill|Plants of the World Online|en|Plants of the World Online|WD=Q47542613|lt=Plants of the World Online|1=Plants of the World Online}} accepted four species: {| class="wikitable" |- ! All parts of the plant contain a {{ill|saponin|en|saponin|WD=Q207653|lt=saponin|1=Saponin}} called wisterin, which is {{ill|Toxicity|en|Toxicity|WD=Q274160|lt=toxic|1=Toxicity}} if ingested, and may cause {{ill|dizziness|en|dizziness|WD=Q10916362|lt=dizziness|1=Dizziness}}, confusion, speech problems, nausea, {{ill|Vomiting|en|Vomiting|WD=Q127076|lt=Vomiting|1=Vomiting}}, stomach pains, {{ill|Diarrhea|en|Diarrhea|WD=Q40878|lt=Diarrhea|1=Diarrhea}} and collapse. There is debate over whether the concentration outside of the seeds is sufficient to cause poisoning. Wisteria seeds have caused poisoning in children and pets of many countries, producing mild to severe gastroenteritis and other effects. ==Cultivation== {{multiple image |align=right |direction=horizontal |header_align=center |header= |image1=Wisteria at Nymans Gardens, West Sussex, England May 2006.JPG |width1=200 |alt1= |caption1=Wisteria at {{ill|Nymans|en|Nymans|WD=Q7071172|lt=Nymans|1=Nymans}} Gardens
({{ill|West Sussex|en|West Sussex|WD=Q23287|lt=West Sussex|1=West Sussex}}, England) |image2=Climbing_wisteria_(Stresa,_Italy).jpg |width2=200 |alt2= |caption2=Trunk of mature wisteria supported by balustrade ({{ill|Stresa|en|Stresa|WD=Q23700|lt=Stresa|1=Stresa}}, Italy) }} In North America, ''{{ill|Wisteria floribunda|en|Wisteria floribunda|WD=Q1329209|lt=W. floribunda|1=Wisteria floribunda}}'' (Japanese wisteria) and ''{{ill|Wisteria sinensis|en|Wisteria sinensis|WD=Q159116|lt=W. sinensis|1=Wisteria sinensis}}'' (Chinese wisteria) are far more popular than other species for their abundance of flowers, clusters of large flowers, variety of flower colors, and fragrance. ''W. sinensis'' was brought to the United States for horticultural purposes in 1816, while ''W. floribunda'' was introduced around 1830. Because of their hardiness and tendency to {{ill|escaped plant|en|escaped plant|WD=Q1494641|lt=escape cultivation|1=Escaped plant}}, these non-native wisterias are considered {{ill|Invasive species|en|Invasive species|WD=Q183368|lt=Invasive species|1=Invasive species}} in many parts of the {{ill|United States|en|United States|WD=Q30|lt=U.S.|1=United States}}, especially the {{ill|Southeastern United States|en|Southeastern United States|WD=Q1139046|lt=Southeast|1=Southeastern United States}}, due to their ability to overtake and choke out other native plant species. ''{{ill|Wisteria floribunda|en|Wisteria floribunda|WD=Q1329209|lt=W. floribunda|1=Wisteria floribunda}}'' (Japanese wisteria), which has the longest racemes of wisteria species, is decorative and has given rise to many {{ill|Cultivar|en|Cultivar|WD=Q4886|lt=Cultivar|1=Cultivar}}s that have won the prestigious {{ill|Award of Garden Merit|en|Award of Garden Merit|WD=Q3501416|lt=Award of Garden Merit|1=Award of Garden Merit}}. Wisteria, especially ''{{ill|Wisteria sinensis|en|Wisteria sinensis|WD=Q159116|lt=W. sinensis|1=Wisteria sinensis}}'' (Chinese wisteria), is very hardy and fast-growing. It can grow in fairly poor-quality soils, but prefers fertile, moist, well-drained soil. It thrives in full sun. It can be propagated via hardwood cutting, softwood cuttings, or seed. However, specimens grown from seed can take decades to bloom; for this reason, gardeners usually grow plants that have been started from rooted cuttings or grafted {{ill|Cultivar|en|Cultivar|WD=Q4886|lt=Cultivar|1=Cultivar}}s known to flower well. Another reason for failure to bloom can be excessive fertilizer (particularly {{ill|nitrogen|en|nitrogen|WD=Q627|lt=nitrogen|1=Nitrogen}}). Wisteria has nitrogen fixing capability (provided by ''{{ill|Rhizobia|en|Rhizobia|WD=Q9164450|lt=Rhizobia|1=Rhizobia}}'' bacteria in root nodules), and thus mature plants may benefit from added {{ill|potassium|en|potassium|WD=Q703|lt=potassium|1=Potassium}} and {{ill|phosphate|en|phosphate|WD=Q46220103|lt=phosphate|1=Phosphate}}, but not nitrogen. Finally, wisteria can be reluctant to bloom before it has reached maturity. Maturation may require only a few years, as in ''{{ill|Wisteria macrostachya|en|Wisteria macrostachya|WD=Q8027752|lt=W. macrostachya|1=Wisteria macrostachya}}'' (Kentucky wisteria), or nearly twenty, as in ''W. sinensis''. Maturation can be forced by physically abusing the main {{ill|Trunk (botany)|en|Trunk (botany)|WD=Q193472|lt=trunk|1=Trunk (botany)}}, root pruning, or {{ill|Drought|en|Drought|WD=Q43059|lt=Drought|1=Drought}} stress. Wisteria can grow into a mound when unsupported, but is at its best when allowed to clamber up a tree, {{ill|pergola|en|pergola|WD=Q264458|lt=pergola|1=Pergola}}, wall, or other supporting structure. ''W. floribunda'' (Japanese wisteria) with longer racemes is the best choice to grow along a pergola. ''W. sinensis'' (Chinese wisteria) with shorter racemes is the best choice for growing along a wall. Whatever the case, the support must be very sturdy, because mature wisteria can become immensely strong with heavy wrist-thick {{ill|Trunk (botany)|en|Trunk (botany)|WD=Q193472|lt=trunk|1=Trunk (botany)}}s and {{ill|Plant stem|en|Plant stem|WD=Q134267|lt=stem|1=Plant stem}}s. These can collapse latticework, crush thin wooden posts, and even strangle large trees. Wisteria allowed to grow on houses can cause damage to gutters, downspouts, and similar structures. Wisteria flowers develop in buds near the base of the previous year's growth, so {{ill|pruning|en|pruning|WD=Q500094|lt=pruning|1=Pruning}} back side shoots to the basal few buds in early spring can enhance the visibility of the flowers. If it is desired to control the size of the plant, the side shoots can be shortened to between 20 and 40 cm long in midsummer, and back to {{convert|10|to|20|cm}} in the fall. Once the plant is a few years old, a relatively compact, free-flowering form can be achieved by pruning off the new tendrils three times during the growing season in the summer months. The flowers of some varieties are edible, and can even be used to make wine. Others are said to be toxic. Careful identification by an expert is strongly recommended before consuming this or any wild plant. In the United Kingdom, the national collection of wisteria is held by Chris Lane at the Witch Hazel Nursery in {{ill|Newington, Swale|en|Newington, Swale|WD=Q10748183|lt=Newington|1=Newington, Swale}}, near {{ill|Sittingbourne|en|Sittingbourne|WD=Q1626044|lt=Sittingbourne|1=Sittingbourne}} in {{ill|Kent|en|Kent|WD=Q23298|lt=Kent|1=Kent}}. {{Clear}} ==Art and symbolism== [[File:Sagari Fuji (No background and Black color drawing).svg|thumb|right|150px|{{transliteration|ja|Sagari fuji mon}} (Wisteria {{transliteration|ja|[[Mon (emblem)|mon]]}})]] Wisteria and their racemes have been widely used in Japan throughout the centuries and were a popular symbol in {{nihongo3|family crests||[[Mon (emblem)|mon]]}} and heraldry. Wisteria is one of the five most commonly used motifs in the {{transliteration|ja|mon}}, and there are more than 150 types of wisteria {{transliteration|ja|mon}}. Because of its longevity and fertility, wisteria was considered an auspicious plant and was favored as a {{transliteration|ja|mon}}, and was adopted and popularized by the [[Fujiwara clan]] as their {{transliteration|ja|mon}}.{{cite web|url=https://www.nippon.com/en/japan-data/h01578/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230420034414/https://www.nippon.com/en/japan-data/h01578/|title="Kamon": Japan's Family Crests|publisher=nippon.com|date=10 February 2023|archive-date=20 April 2023|access-date=29 April 2023}}{{cite web|url=https://irohakamon.com/kamon/fuji/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230212111436/https://irohakamon.com/kamon/fuji/|script-title=ja:藤紋（ふじ）について|language=ja|publisher=Kamon no iroha|archive-date=12 February 2023|access-date=29 April 2023}} {{multiple image |direction=horizontal |width1=147 |width2=150 |align=left |footer=Left to right: ''View of Oyster Bay'' (1908), by [[:en:Louis C. Tiffany|Louis C. Tiffany]], with wisteria evoking the estate of its patrons, {{ill|Wistariahurst|en|Wistariahurst|WD=Q8027742|lt=Wistariahurst|1=Wistariahurst}}; ''Japanese wisteria and white-bellied green pigeons'' (1883), a woodblock print by {{ill|Kōno Bairei|en|Kōno Bairei|WD=Q3201302|lt=Kōno Bairei|1=Kōno Bairei}} |image1=At the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York 2017 04 - View of Oyster Bay. New York City.jpg |image2=Bairei kachō gafu, Spring 12, Japanese wisteria and white-bellied green pigeons.jpg}} One popular dance in {{ill|Kabuki|en|Kabuki|WD=Q199701|lt=Kabuki|1=Kabuki}} known as the ''{{ill|Fuji Musume|en|Fuji Musume|WD=Q11623783|lt=Fuji Musume|1=Fuji Musume}}'' (or 'The Wisteria Maiden'), is the sole extant dance of a series of five personifying dances in which a maiden becomes the embodiment of the spirit of wisteria. In the West, both in building materials such as tile, as well as stained glass, wisterias have been used both in realism and stylistically in artistic works and industrial design. {{Clear}} ==References== {{Reflist|refs= {{cite book |last=Baird |first=Merrily C. |year=2001 |title=Symbols of Japan: Thematic Motifs in Art and Design |publisher=Random House, Inc. |location=New York |page=67 |oclc=237418692}} {{cite book |last=Bryson |first=Bill |author-link=Bill Bryson |title=A Short History of Nearly Everything |edition=1st |year=2003 |publisher=Broadway Books |location=New York, NY |isbn=0-375-43200-0 |chapter=Ch. 6 — Science Red in Tooth and Claw |url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780375432002}} {{cite web |last=Charters |first=Michael L. |work=California Plant Names: Latin and Greek Meanings and Derivations |title=Page W |url=http://www.calflora.net/botanicalnames/pageW.html |access-date=2011-05-15}} {{Cite journal |last1=Compton |first1=James A. |last2=Schrire |first2=Brian D. |last3=Könyves |first3=Kálmán |last4=Forest |first4=Félix |last5=Malakasi |first5=Panagiota |last6=Sawai Mattapha |last7=Sirichamorn |first7=Yotsawate |date=2019 |title=The ''Callerya'' Group redefined and Tribe Wisterieae (Fabaceae) emended based on morphology and data from nuclear and chloroplast DNA sequences |journal=PhytoKeys |issue=125 |pages=1–112 |doi=10.3897/phytokeys.125.34877 |pmid=31303810 |pmc=6610001 |name-list-style=amp |doi-access=free }} {{cite book |last1=Cotter |first1=John L. |last2=Roberts |first2=Daniel G. |last3=Parrington |first3=Michael |year=1994 |title=The Buried Past: An Archaeological History of Philadelphia |publication-place=Philadelphia |publisher=University of Pennsylvania Press |page=339 |name-list-style=amp}} {{Cite web |date=15 April 2014 |title=Canadian Poisonous Plants Information System - needed|date=June 2024}}{{Automatic taxobox |image = Chinese Wisteria Blütentrauben.JPG |image_caption = Flowering ''{{ill|Wisteria sinensis|en|Wisteria sinensis|WD=Q159116|lt=Wisteria sinensis|1=Wisteria sinensis}}'' |taxon = Wisteria |authority = {{ill|Thomas Nuttall|en|Thomas Nuttall|WD=Q728337|lt=Nutt.|1=Thomas Nuttall}} (1818), nom. cons. |synonyms = * ''Bradburia'' {{small|Spreng. (1826)}} * ''Diplonyx'' Raf. (1817), nom. rej. * ''Kraunhia'' Raf. (1891), nom. superfl. * ''Phaseoloides'' Duhamel (1755), nom. rej. * ''Rehsonia'' Stritch (1984) * ''Thyrsanthus'' {{small|Elliott (1818), nom. illeg.}} * ''Wistaria'' {{small|Nutt. ex Spreng. (1826), orth. var.}} |synonyms_ref = }} '''''Wisteria''''' is a {{ill|Genus|en|Genus|WD=Q34740|lt=Genus|1=Genus}} of {{ill|Flowering plant|en|Flowering plant|WD=Q25314|lt=Flowering plant|1=Flowering plant}}s in the {{ill|legume|en|legume|WD=Q145909|lt=legume|1=Legume}} family, {{ill|Fabaceae|en|Fabaceae|WD=Q44448|lt=Fabaceae|1=Fabaceae}} (Leguminosae). The genus includes four species of woody twining vines that are native to {{ill|China|en|China|WD=Q148|lt=China|1=China}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}, {{ill|Korea|en|Korea|WD=Q18097|lt=Korea|1=Korea}}, {{ill|Vietnam|en|Vietnam|WD=Q881|lt=Vietnam|1=Vietnam}}, southern {{ill|Canada|en|Canada|WD=Q16|lt=Canada|1=Canada}}, the {{ill|Eastern United States|en|Eastern United States|WD=Q1189650|lt=Eastern United States|1=Eastern United States}}, and north of {{ill|Iran|en|Iran|WD=Q794|lt=Iran|1=Iran}}. They were later introduced to France, Germany and various other countries in Europe. Some species are popular ornamental plants. The genus name is also used as the English name, and may then be spelt 'wistaria'. In some countries in Western and Central Europe, ''Wisteria'' is also known by a variant spelling of the {{ill|Genus|en|Genus|WD=Q34740|lt=Genus|1=Genus}} in which species were formerly placed, ''{{ill|Glycine (plant)|en|Glycine (plant)|WD=Q311395|lt=Glycine|1=Glycine (plant)}}''. Examples include the French ''glycines'', the German ''Glyzinie'', and the Polish ''glicynia''. The aquatic flowering plant commonly called wisteria or 'water wisteria' is ''{{ill|Hygrophila difformis|en|Hygrophila difformis|WD=Q1431832|lt=Hygrophila difformis|1=Hygrophila difformis}}'', in the family {{ill|Acanthaceae|en|Acanthaceae|WD=Q53475|lt=Acanthaceae|1=Acanthaceae}}. ==Description== [[File:Wisteria floribunda MHNT.BOT.2008.1.38.jpg|right|thumb|Seeds and seedpods of ''{{ill|Wisteria floribunda|en|Wisteria floribunda|WD=Q1329209|lt=Wisteria floribunda|1=Wisteria floribunda}}'' (Japanese wisteria). The seeds of all ''Wisteria'' species contain high levels of the [[:en:wisterin|wisterin]] toxin and are especially poisonous.]] Wisterias climb by twining their {{ill|Plant stem|en|Plant stem|WD=Q134267|lt=stem|1=Plant stem}}s around any available support. ''{{ill|Wisteria floribunda|en|Wisteria floribunda|WD=Q1329209|lt=W. floribunda|1=Wisteria floribunda}}'' (Japanese wisteria) twines clockwise when viewed from above, while ''{{ill|Wisteria sinensis|en|Wisteria sinensis|WD=Q159116|lt=W. sinensis|1=Wisteria sinensis}}'' (Chinese wisteria) twines counterclockwise. This is an aid in identifying the two most common species of wisteria. They can climb as high as {{convert|20|m|ft|abbr=on}} above the ground and spread out {{convert|10|m|ft|abbr=on}} laterally. The world's largest known wisteria is the [[:en:Sierra Madre Wisteria|Sierra Madre Wisteria]] in {{ill|Sierra Madre, California|en|Sierra Madre, California|WD=Q174026|lt=Sierra Madre, California|1=Sierra Madre, California}}, measuring more than {{convert|1|acre|ha}} in size and weighing 250 tons. Planted in 1894, it is of the 'Chinese lavender' variety. The {{ill|Leaf|en|Leaf|WD=Q33971|lt=leaves|1=Leaf}} are alternate, 15 to 35 cm long, {{ill|Pinnation|en|Pinnation|WD=Q3756157|lt=pinnate|1=Pinnation}}, with 9 to 19 leaflets. The {{ill|Flower|en|Flower|WD=Q506|lt=Flower|1=Flower}}s have drooping {{ill|raceme|en|raceme|WD=Q158583|lt=raceme|1=Raceme}}s that vary in length from species to species. ''{{ill|Wisteria frutescens|en|Wisteria frutescens|WD=Q8027753|lt=W. frutescens|1=Wisteria frutescens}}'' (American wisteria) has the shortest racemes, {{convert|5|–|7|cm}}. ''W. floribunda'' (Japanese wisteria) has the longest racemes, {{convert|90|cm}} in some {{ill|Variety (botany)|en|Variety (botany)|WD=Q767728|lt=varieties|1=Variety (botany)}} and {{convert|120|cm}} or {{convert|200|cm}} in some [[:en:cultivars|cultivars]]. The flowers come in a variety of colors, including white, lilac, purple, and pink, and some ''{{ill|Wisteria brachybotrys|en|Wisteria brachybotrys|WD=Q5783537|lt=W. brachybotrys|1=Wisteria brachybotrys}}'' (Silky wisteria) and ''W. floribunda'' cultivars have particularly remarkable colors. The flowers are fragrant, and especially cultivars of ''W. brachybotrys'', ''W. floribunda'', and ''W. sinensis'' are noted for their sweet and musky scents. Flowering is in spring (just before or as the leaves open) in some Asian species, and in mid to late summer in the American species. ==Taxonomy== {{See also|Wisterieae#Taxonomy}} The genus ''Wisteria'' was established by {{ill|Thomas Nuttall|en|Thomas Nuttall|WD=Q728337|lt=Thomas Nuttall|1=Thomas Nuttall}} in 1818. He based the genus on ''{{ill|Wisteria frutescens|en|Wisteria frutescens|WD=Q8027753|lt=Wisteria frutescens|1=Wisteria frutescens}}'', previously included in the genus ''{{ill|Glycine (plant)|en|Glycine (plant)|WD=Q311395|lt=Glycine|1=Glycine (plant)}}''. Nuttall stated that he named the genus in memory of the American physician and anatomist {{ill|Caspar Wistar (physician)|en|Caspar Wistar (physician)|WD=Q347595|lt=Caspar Wistar|1=Caspar Wistar (physician)}} (1761–1818). Both men were living in Philadelphia at the time, where Wistar was a professor in the [[:en:Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania|School of Medicine]] at the {{ill|University of Pennsylvania|en|University of Pennsylvania|WD=Q49117|lt=University of Pennsylvania|1=University of Pennsylvania}}. Questioned about the spelling later, Nuttall said it was for "[[:en:euphony|euphony]]", but his biographer speculated that it may have something to do with Nuttall's friend Charles Jones Wister Sr., of {{ill|Grumblethorpe|en|Grumblethorpe|WD=Q5612044|lt=Grumblethorpe|1=Grumblethorpe}}, the grandson of the merchant [[John Wister]]. Various sources assert that the naming occurred in {{ill|Philadelphia|en|Philadelphia|WD=Q1345|lt=Philadelphia|1=Philadelphia}}. It has been suggested that the Portuguese botanist and geologist {{ill|José Correia da Serra|en|José Correia da Serra|WD=Q2656605|lt=José Francisco Corrêa da Serra|1=José Correia da Serra}}, who lived in Philadelphia beginning in 1812, four years before his appointment as ambassador of {{ill|Portugal|en|Portugal|WD=Q45|lt=Portugal|1=Portugal}} to the United States, and a friend of Wistar, proposed the name "Wistaria" in his obituary of Wistar. As the spelling is apparently deliberate, there is no justification for changing the genus name under the {{ill|International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants|en|International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants|WD=Q693148|lt=International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants|1=International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants}}. ===Classification=== The genus was previously placed in the tribe {{ill|Millettieae|en|Millettieae|WD=Q141908|lt=Millettieae|1=Millettieae}}. {{ill|Molecular phylogenetics|en|Molecular phylogenetics|WD=Q2007033|lt=Molecular phylogenetic|1=Molecular phylogenetics}} studies from 2000 onwards showed that ''Wisteria'', along with other genera such as ''{{ill|Callerya|en|Callerya|WD=Q2705210|lt=Callerya|1=Callerya}}'' and ''{{ill|Afgekia|en|Afgekia|WD=Q3310234|lt=Afgekia|1=Afgekia}}'', were related and quite distinct from other members of the Millettieae. A more detailed study in 2019 reached the same conclusion, and moved ''Wisteria'' to the expanded tribe {{ill|Wisterieae|en|Wisterieae|WD=Q92314202|lt=Wisterieae|1=Wisterieae}}. ===Species=== [[File:足利の藤 (Wisteria trellises in Ashikaga) 29 Apr, 2009 - panoramio.jpg|thumb|250x250px|''W. floribunda'' at [[Ashikaga Flower Park]] ([[:ja:あしかがフラワーパーク|ja]]) in {{lang|ja-Latn|{{ill|Ashikaga, Tochigi|en|Ashikaga, Tochigi|WD=Q374477|lt=Ashikaga, Tochigi|1=Ashikaga, Tochigi}}|italic=no}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}. The largest wisteria in Japan, it is dated to {{circa|1870}} and covered approximately {{convert|1,990|sqm}} {{as of|May 2008|lc=true}}.|alt=]] {{As of|2023|September}}, {{ill|Plants of the World Online|en|Plants of the World Online|WD=Q47542613|lt=Plants of the World Online|1=Plants of the World Online}} accepted four species: {| class="wikitable" |- ! Image !! Scientific name !! Common Name !! Distribution |- |[[File:Wisteria brachybotrys 03.jpg|120px]] ||''{{ill|Wisteria brachybotrys|en|Wisteria brachybotrys|WD=Q5783537|lt=Wisteria brachybotrys|1=Wisteria brachybotrys}}'' Siebold & Zucc. (syn. ''Wisteria venusta'' Rehder & Wils.) || Silky wisteria || Japan |- |[[File:20130514Wisteria floribunda7.jpg|120px]] ||''{{ill|Wisteria floribunda|en|Wisteria floribunda|WD=Q1329209|lt=Wisteria floribunda|1=Wisteria floribunda}}'' ([[:en:Carl Ludwig von Willdenow|Willd.]]) {{ill|Augustin Pyramus de Candolle|en|Augustin Pyramus de Candolle|WD=Q123057|lt=DC.|1=Augustin Pyramus de Candolle}} || Japanese wisteria || Japan |- |[[File:Wisteria frutescens flower closeup.jpg|120px]] ||''{{ill|Wisteria frutescens|en|Wisteria frutescens|WD=Q8027753|lt=Wisteria frutescens|1=Wisteria frutescens}}'' ({{ill|Carl Linnaeus|en|Carl Linnaeus|WD=Q1043|lt=L.|1=Carl Linnaeus}}) {{ill|Jean Louis Marie Poiret|en|Jean Louis Marie Poiret|WD=Q966539|lt=Poir.|1=Jean Louis Marie Poiret}} (syn. ''Wisteria macrostachys'') || American wisteria || United States (Kentucky to Texas, to Florida, as well as Iowa, Michigan, and New York) |- |[[File:Wisteria sinensis 5Dsr 0101.jpg|120px]] ||''{{ill|Wisteria sinensis|en|Wisteria sinensis|WD=Q159116|lt=Wisteria sinensis|1=Wisteria sinensis}}'' ({{ill|John Sims (taxonomist)|en|John Sims (taxonomist)|WD=Q2430593|lt=Sims|1=John Sims (taxonomist)}}) DC. || Chinese wisteria || China (Guangxi, Guizhou, Hebei, Henan, Hubei, Shaanxi, and Yunnan.) |} {{Clear}} ==Ecology== {{Unreferenced section|date=May 2024}} ''Wisteria'' species are used as food by the {{ill|larva|en|larva|WD=Q129270|lt=larva|1=Larva}}e of some {{ill|Lepidoptera|en|Lepidoptera|WD=Q28319|lt=Lepidoptera|1=Lepidoptera}} species including the {{ill|brown-tail moth|en|brown-tail moth|WD=Q45902|lt=brown-tail moth|1=Brown-tail moth}}. ==Toxicity== The {{ill|Seed|en|Seed|WD=Q40763|lt=Seed|1=Seed}}s are produced in pods similar to those of ''Laburnum'', and, like the seeds of that genus, are {{ill|poison|en|poison|WD=Q40867|lt=poison|1=Poison}}ous. All parts of the plant contain a {{ill|saponin|en|saponin|WD=Q207653|lt=saponin|1=Saponin}} called wisterin, which is {{ill|Toxicity|en|Toxicity|WD=Q274160|lt=toxic|1=Toxicity}} if ingested, and may cause {{ill|dizziness|en|dizziness|WD=Q10916362|lt=dizziness|1=Dizziness}}, confusion, speech problems, nausea, {{ill|Vomiting|en|Vomiting|WD=Q127076|lt=Vomiting|1=Vomiting}}, stomach pains, {{ill|Diarrhea|en|Diarrhea|WD=Q40878|lt=Diarrhea|1=Diarrhea}} and collapse. There is debate over whether the concentration outside of the seeds is sufficient to cause poisoning. Wisteria seeds have caused poisoning in children and pets of many countries, producing mild to severe gastroenteritis and other effects. ==Cultivation== {{multiple image |align=right |direction=horizontal |header_align=center |header= |image1=Wisteria at Nymans Gardens, West Sussex, England May 2006.JPG |width1=200 |alt1= |caption1=Wisteria at {{ill|Nymans|en|Nymans|WD=Q7071172|lt=Nymans|1=Nymans}} Gardens
({{ill|West Sussex|en|West Sussex|WD=Q23287|lt=West Sussex|1=West Sussex}}, England) |image2=Climbing_wisteria_(Stresa,_Italy).jpg |width2=200 |alt2= |caption2=Trunk of mature wisteria supported by balustrade ({{ill|Stresa|en|Stresa|WD=Q23700|lt=Stresa|1=Stresa}}, Italy) }} In North America, ''{{ill|Wisteria floribunda|en|Wisteria floribunda|WD=Q1329209|lt=W. floribunda|1=Wisteria floribunda}}'' (Japanese wisteria) and ''{{ill|Wisteria sinensis|en|Wisteria sinensis|WD=Q159116|lt=W. sinensis|1=Wisteria sinensis}}'' (Chinese wisteria) are far more popular than other species for their abundance of flowers, clusters of large flowers, variety of flower colors, and fragrance. ''W. sinensis'' was brought to the United States for horticultural purposes in 1816, while ''W. floribunda'' was introduced around 1830. Because of their hardiness and tendency to {{ill|escaped plant|en|escaped plant|WD=Q1494641|lt=escape cultivation|1=Escaped plant}}, these non-native wisterias are considered {{ill|Invasive species|en|Invasive species|WD=Q183368|lt=Invasive species|1=Invasive species}} in many parts of the {{ill|United States|en|United States|WD=Q30|lt=U.S.|1=United States}}, especially the {{ill|Southeastern United States|en|Southeastern United States|WD=Q1139046|lt=Southeast|1=Southeastern United States}}, due to their ability to overtake and choke out other native plant species. ''{{ill|Wisteria floribunda|en|Wisteria floribunda|WD=Q1329209|lt=W. floribunda|1=Wisteria floribunda}}'' (Japanese wisteria), which has the longest racemes of wisteria species, is decorative and has given rise to many {{ill|Cultivar|en|Cultivar|WD=Q4886|lt=Cultivar|1=Cultivar}}s that have won the prestigious {{ill|Award of Garden Merit|en|Award of Garden Merit|WD=Q3501416|lt=Award of Garden Merit|1=Award of Garden Merit}}. Wisteria, especially ''{{ill|Wisteria sinensis|en|Wisteria sinensis|WD=Q159116|lt=W. sinensis|1=Wisteria sinensis}}'' (Chinese wisteria), is very hardy and fast-growing. It can grow in fairly poor-quality soils, but prefers fertile, moist, well-drained soil. It thrives in full sun. It can be propagated via hardwood cutting, softwood cuttings, or seed. However, specimens grown from seed can take decades to bloom; for this reason, gardeners usually grow plants that have been started from rooted cuttings or grafted {{ill|Cultivar|en|Cultivar|WD=Q4886|lt=Cultivar|1=Cultivar}}s known to flower well. Another reason for failure to bloom can be excessive fertilizer (particularly {{ill|nitrogen|en|nitrogen|WD=Q627|lt=nitrogen|1=Nitrogen}}). Wisteria has nitrogen fixing capability (provided by ''{{ill|Rhizobia|en|Rhizobia|WD=Q9164450|lt=Rhizobia|1=Rhizobia}}'' bacteria in root nodules), and thus mature plants may benefit from added {{ill|potassium|en|potassium|WD=Q703|lt=potassium|1=Potassium}} and {{ill|phosphate|en|phosphate|WD=Q46220103|lt=phosphate|1=Phosphate}}, but not nitrogen. Finally, wisteria can be reluctant to bloom before it has reached maturity. Maturation may require only a few years, as in ''{{ill|Wisteria macrostachya|en|Wisteria macrostachya|WD=Q8027752|lt=W. macrostachya|1=Wisteria macrostachya}}'' (Kentucky wisteria), or nearly twenty, as in ''W. sinensis''. Maturation can be forced by physically abusing the main {{ill|Trunk (botany)|en|Trunk (botany)|WD=Q193472|lt=trunk|1=Trunk (botany)}}, root pruning, or {{ill|Drought|en|Drought|WD=Q43059|lt=Drought|1=Drought}} stress. Wisteria can grow into a mound when unsupported, but is at its best when allowed to clamber up a tree, {{ill|pergola|en|pergola|WD=Q264458|lt=pergola|1=Pergola}}, wall, or other supporting structure. ''W. floribunda'' (Japanese wisteria) with longer racemes is the best choice to grow along a pergola. ''W. sinensis'' (Chinese wisteria) with shorter racemes is the best choice for growing along a wall. Whatever the case, the support must be very sturdy, because mature wisteria can become immensely strong with heavy wrist-thick {{ill|Trunk (botany)|en|Trunk (botany)|WD=Q193472|lt=trunk|1=Trunk (botany)}}s and {{ill|Plant stem|en|Plant stem|WD=Q134267|lt=stem|1=Plant stem}}s. These can collapse latticework, crush thin wooden posts, and even strangle large trees. Wisteria allowed to grow on houses can cause damage to gutters, downspouts, and similar structures. Wisteria flowers develop in buds near the base of the previous year's growth, so {{ill|pruning|en|pruning|WD=Q500094|lt=pruning|1=Pruning}} back side shoots to the basal few buds in early spring can enhance the visibility of the flowers. If it is desired to control the size of the plant, the side shoots can be shortened to between 20 and 40 cm long in midsummer, and back to {{convert|10|to|20|cm}} in the fall. Once the plant is a few years old, a relatively compact, free-flowering form can be achieved by pruning off the new tendrils three times during the growing season in the summer months. The flowers of some varieties are edible, and can even be used to make wine. Others are said to be toxic. Careful identification by an expert is strongly recommended before consuming this or any wild plant. In the United Kingdom, the national collection of wisteria is held by Chris Lane at the Witch Hazel Nursery in {{ill|Newington, Swale|en|Newington, Swale|WD=Q10748183|lt=Newington|1=Newington, Swale}}, near {{ill|Sittingbourne|en|Sittingbourne|WD=Q1626044|lt=Sittingbourne|1=Sittingbourne}} in {{ill|Kent|en|Kent|WD=Q23298|lt=Kent|1=Kent}}. {{Clear}} ==Art and symbolism== [[File:Sagari Fuji (No background and Black color drawing).svg|thumb|right|150px|{{transliteration|ja|Sagari fuji mon}} (Wisteria {{transliteration|ja|[[Mon (emblem)|mon]]}})]] Wisteria and their racemes have been widely used in Japan throughout the centuries and were a popular symbol in {{nihongo3|family crests||[[Mon (emblem)|mon]]}} and heraldry. Wisteria is one of the five most commonly used motifs in the {{transliteration|ja|mon}}, and there are more than 150 types of wisteria {{transliteration|ja|mon}}. Because of its longevity and fertility, wisteria was considered an auspicious plant and was favored as a {{transliteration|ja|mon}}, and was adopted and popularized by the [[Fujiwara clan]] as their {{transliteration|ja|mon}}.{{cite web|url=https://www.nippon.com/en/japan-data/h01578/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230420034414/https://www.nippon.com/en/japan-data/h01578/|title="Kamon": Japan's Family Crests|publisher=nippon.com|date=10 February 2023|archive-date=20 April 2023|access-date=29 April 2023}}{{cite web|url=https://irohakamon.com/kamon/fuji/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230212111436/https://irohakamon.com/kamon/fuji/|script-title=ja:藤紋（ふじ）について|language=ja|publisher=Kamon no iroha|archive-date=12 February 2023|access-date=29 April 2023}} {{multiple image |direction=horizontal |width1=147 |width2=150 |align=left |footer=Left to right: ''View of Oyster Bay'' (1908), by [[:en:Louis C. Tiffany|Louis C. Tiffany]], with wisteria evoking the estate of its patrons, {{ill|Wistariahurst|en|Wistariahurst|WD=Q8027742|lt=Wistariahurst|1=Wistariahurst}}; ''Japanese wisteria and white-bellied green pigeons'' (1883), a woodblock print by {{ill|Kōno Bairei|en|Kōno Bairei|WD=Q3201302|lt=Kōno Bairei|1=Kōno Bairei}} |image1=At the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York 2017 04 - View of Oyster Bay. New York City.jpg |image2=Bairei kachō gafu, Spring 12, Japanese wisteria and white-bellied green pigeons.jpg}} One popular dance in {{ill|Kabuki|en|Kabuki|WD=Q199701|lt=Kabuki|1=Kabuki}} known as the ''{{ill|Fuji Musume|en|Fuji Musume|WD=Q11623783|lt=Fuji Musume|1=Fuji Musume}}'' (or 'The Wisteria Maiden'), is the sole extant dance of a series of five personifying dances in which a maiden becomes the embodiment of the spirit of wisteria. In the West, both in building materials such as tile, as well as stained glass, wisterias have been used both in realism and stylistically in artistic works and industrial design. {{Clear}} ==References== {{Reflist|refs= {{cite book |last=Baird |first=Merrily C. |year=2001 |title=Symbols of Japan: Thematic Motifs in Art and Design |publisher=Random House, Inc. |location=New York |page=67 |oclc=237418692}} {{cite book |last=Bryson |first=Bill |author-link=Bill Bryson |title=A Short History of Nearly Everything |edition=1st |year=2003 |publisher=Broadway Books |location=New York, NY |isbn=0-375-43200-0 |chapter=Ch. 6 — Science Red in Tooth and Claw |url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780375432002}} {{cite web |last=Charters |first=Michael L. |work=California Plant Names: Latin and Greek Meanings and Derivations |title=Page W |url=http://www.calflora.net/botanicalnames/pageW.html |access-date=2011-05-15}} {{Cite journal |last1=Compton |first1=James A. |last2=Schrire |first2=Brian D. |last3=Könyves |first3=Kálmán |last4=Forest |first4=Félix |last5=Malakasi |first5=Panagiota |last6=Sawai Mattapha |last7=Sirichamorn |first7=Yotsawate |date=2019 |title=The ''Callerya'' Group redefined and Tribe Wisterieae (Fabaceae) emended based on morphology and data from nuclear and chloroplast DNA sequences |journal=PhytoKeys |issue=125 |pages=1–112 |doi=10.3897/phytokeys.125.34877 |pmid=31303810 |pmc=6610001 |name-list-style=amp |doi-access=free }} {{cite book |last1=Cotter |first1=John L. |last2=Roberts |first2=Daniel G. |last3=Parrington |first3=Michael |year=1994 |title=The Buried Past: An Archaeological History of Philadelphia |publication-place=Philadelphia |publisher=University of Pennsylvania Press |page=339 |name-list-style=amp}} {{Cite web |date=15 April 2014 |title=Canadian Poisonous Plants Information System - (1826), orth. var.}} |synonyms_ref = }} '''''Wisteria''''' is a {{ill|Genus|en|Genus|WD=Q34740|lt=Genus|1=Genus}} of {{ill|Flowering plant|en|Flowering plant|WD=Q25314|lt=Flowering plant|1=Flowering plant}}s in the {{ill|legume|en|legume|WD=Q145909|lt=legume|1=Legume}} family, {{ill|Fabaceae|en|Fabaceae|WD=Q44448|lt=Fabaceae|1=Fabaceae}} (Leguminosae). The genus includes four species of woody twining vines that are native to {{ill|China|en|China|WD=Q148|lt=China|1=China}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}, {{ill|Korea|en|Korea|WD=Q18097|lt=Korea|1=Korea}}, {{ill|Vietnam|en|Vietnam|WD=Q881|lt=Vietnam|1=Vietnam}}, southern {{ill|Canada|en|Canada|WD=Q16|lt=Canada|1=Canada}}, the {{ill|Eastern United States|en|Eastern United States|WD=Q1189650|lt=Eastern United States|1=Eastern United States}}, and north of {{ill|Iran|en|Iran|WD=Q794|lt=Iran|1=Iran}}. They were later introduced to France, Germany and various other countries in Europe. Some species are popular ornamental plants. The genus name is also used as the English name, and may then be spelt 'wistaria'. In some countries in Western and Central Europe, ''Wisteria'' is also known by a variant spelling of the {{ill|Genus|en|Genus|WD=Q34740|lt=Genus|1=Genus}} in which species were formerly placed, ''{{ill|Glycine (plant)|en|Glycine (plant)|WD=Q311395|lt=Glycine|1=Glycine (plant)}}''. Examples include the French ''glycines'', the German ''Glyzinie'', and the Polish ''glicynia''. The aquatic flowering plant commonly called wisteria or 'water wisteria' is ''{{ill|Hygrophila difformis|en|Hygrophila difformis|WD=Q1431832|lt=Hygrophila difformis|1=Hygrophila difformis}}'', in the family {{ill|Acanthaceae|en|Acanthaceae|WD=Q53475|lt=Acanthaceae|1=Acanthaceae}}. ==Description== [[File:Wisteria floribunda MHNT.BOT.2008.1.38.jpg|right|thumb|Seeds and seedpods of ''{{ill|Wisteria floribunda|en|Wisteria floribunda|WD=Q1329209|lt=Wisteria floribunda|1=Wisteria floribunda}}'' (Japanese wisteria). The seeds of all ''Wisteria'' species contain high levels of the [[:en:wisterin|wisterin]] toxin and are especially poisonous.]] Wisterias climb by twining their {{ill|Plant stem|en|Plant stem|WD=Q134267|lt=stem|1=Plant stem}}s around any available support. ''{{ill|Wisteria floribunda|en|Wisteria floribunda|WD=Q1329209|lt=W. floribunda|1=Wisteria floribunda}}'' (Japanese wisteria) twines clockwise when viewed from above, while ''{{ill|Wisteria sinensis|en|Wisteria sinensis|WD=Q159116|lt=W. sinensis|1=Wisteria sinensis}}'' (Chinese wisteria) twines counterclockwise. This is an aid in identifying the two most common species of wisteria. They can climb as high as {{convert|20|m|ft|abbr=on}} above the ground and spread out {{convert|10|m|ft|abbr=on}} laterally. The world's largest known wisteria is the [[:en:Sierra Madre Wisteria|Sierra Madre Wisteria]] in {{ill|Sierra Madre, California|en|Sierra Madre, California|WD=Q174026|lt=Sierra Madre, California|1=Sierra Madre, California}}, measuring more than {{convert|1|acre|ha}} in size and weighing 250 tons. Planted in 1894, it is of the 'Chinese lavender' variety. The {{ill|Leaf|en|Leaf|WD=Q33971|lt=leaves|1=Leaf}} are alternate, 15 to 35 cm long, {{ill|Pinnation|en|Pinnation|WD=Q3756157|lt=pinnate|1=Pinnation}}, with 9 to 19 leaflets. The {{ill|Flower|en|Flower|WD=Q506|lt=Flower|1=Flower}}s have drooping {{ill|raceme|en|raceme|WD=Q158583|lt=raceme|1=Raceme}}s that vary in length from species to species. ''{{ill|Wisteria frutescens|en|Wisteria frutescens|WD=Q8027753|lt=W. frutescens|1=Wisteria frutescens}}'' (American wisteria) has the shortest racemes, {{convert|5|–|7|cm}}. ''W. floribunda'' (Japanese wisteria) has the longest racemes, {{convert|90|cm}} in some {{ill|Variety (botany)|en|Variety (botany)|WD=Q767728|lt=varieties|1=Variety (botany)}} and {{convert|120|cm}} or {{convert|200|cm}} in some [[:en:cultivars|cultivars]]. The flowers come in a variety of colors, including white, lilac, purple, and pink, and some ''{{ill|Wisteria brachybotrys|en|Wisteria brachybotrys|WD=Q5783537|lt=W. brachybotrys|1=Wisteria brachybotrys}}'' (Silky wisteria) and ''W. floribunda'' cultivars have particularly remarkable colors. The flowers are fragrant, and especially cultivars of ''W. brachybotrys'', ''W. floribunda'', and ''W. sinensis'' are noted for their sweet and musky scents. Flowering is in spring (just before or as the leaves open) in some Asian species, and in mid to late summer in the American species. ==Taxonomy== {{See also|Wisterieae#Taxonomy}} The genus ''Wisteria'' was established by {{ill|Thomas Nuttall|en|Thomas Nuttall|WD=Q728337|lt=Thomas Nuttall|1=Thomas Nuttall}} in 1818. He based the genus on ''{{ill|Wisteria frutescens|en|Wisteria frutescens|WD=Q8027753|lt=Wisteria frutescens|1=Wisteria frutescens}}'', previously included in the genus ''{{ill|Glycine (plant)|en|Glycine (plant)|WD=Q311395|lt=Glycine|1=Glycine (plant)}}''. Nuttall stated that he named the genus in memory of the American physician and anatomist {{ill|Caspar Wistar (physician)|en|Caspar Wistar (physician)|WD=Q347595|lt=Caspar Wistar|1=Caspar Wistar (physician)}} (1761–1818). Both men were living in Philadelphia at the time, where Wistar was a professor in the [[:en:Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania|School of Medicine]] at the {{ill|University of Pennsylvania|en|University of Pennsylvania|WD=Q49117|lt=University of Pennsylvania|1=University of Pennsylvania}}. Questioned about the spelling later, Nuttall said it was for "[[:en:euphony|euphony]]", but his biographer speculated that it may have something to do with Nuttall's friend Charles Jones Wister Sr., of {{ill|Grumblethorpe|en|Grumblethorpe|WD=Q5612044|lt=Grumblethorpe|1=Grumblethorpe}}, the grandson of the merchant [[John Wister]]. Various sources assert that the naming occurred in {{ill|Philadelphia|en|Philadelphia|WD=Q1345|lt=Philadelphia|1=Philadelphia}}. It has been suggested that the Portuguese botanist and geologist {{ill|José Correia da Serra|en|José Correia da Serra|WD=Q2656605|lt=José Francisco Corrêa da Serra|1=José Correia da Serra}}, who lived in Philadelphia beginning in 1812, four years before his appointment as ambassador of {{ill|Portugal|en|Portugal|WD=Q45|lt=Portugal|1=Portugal}} to the United States, and a friend of Wistar, proposed the name "Wistaria" in his obituary of Wistar. As the spelling is apparently deliberate, there is no justification for changing the genus name under the {{ill|International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants|en|International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants|WD=Q693148|lt=International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants|1=International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants}}. ===Classification=== The genus was previously placed in the tribe {{ill|Millettieae|en|Millettieae|WD=Q141908|lt=Millettieae|1=Millettieae}}. {{ill|Molecular phylogenetics|en|Molecular phylogenetics|WD=Q2007033|lt=Molecular phylogenetic|1=Molecular phylogenetics}} studies from 2000 onwards showed that ''Wisteria'', along with other genera such as ''{{ill|Callerya|en|Callerya|WD=Q2705210|lt=Callerya|1=Callerya}}'' and ''{{ill|Afgekia|en|Afgekia|WD=Q3310234|lt=Afgekia|1=Afgekia}}'', were related and quite distinct from other members of the Millettieae. A more detailed study in 2019 reached the same conclusion, and moved ''Wisteria'' to the expanded tribe {{ill|Wisterieae|en|Wisterieae|WD=Q92314202|lt=Wisterieae|1=Wisterieae}}. ===Species=== [[File:足利の藤 (Wisteria trellises in Ashikaga) 29 Apr, 2009 - panoramio.jpg|thumb|250x250px|''W. floribunda'' at [[Ashikaga Flower Park]] ([[:ja:あしかがフラワーパーク|ja]]) in {{lang|ja-Latn|{{ill|Ashikaga, Tochigi|en|Ashikaga, Tochigi|WD=Q374477|lt=Ashikaga, Tochigi|1=Ashikaga, Tochigi}}|italic=no}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}. ''Wisteria macrostachys'') || American wisteria || United States (Kentucky to Texas, to Florida, as well as Iowa, Michigan, and New York) |- |[[File:Wisteria sinensis 5Dsr 0101.jpg|120px]] ||''{{ill|Wisteria sinensis|en|Wisteria sinensis|WD=Q159116|lt=Wisteria sinensis|1=Wisteria sinensis}}'' ({{ill|John Sims (taxonomist)|en|John Sims (taxonomist)|WD=Q2430593|lt=Sims|1=John Sims (taxonomist)}}) DC. || Chinese wisteria || China (Guangxi, Guizhou, Hebei, Henan, Hubei, Shaanxi, and Yunnan.) |} {{Clear}} ==Ecology== {{Unreferenced section|date=May 2024}} ''Wisteria'' species are used as food by the {{ill|larva|en|larva|WD=Q129270|lt=larva|1=Larva}}e of some {{ill|Lepidoptera|en|Lepidoptera|WD=Q28319|lt=Lepidoptera|1=Lepidoptera}} species including the {{ill|brown-tail moth|en|brown-tail moth|WD=Q45902|lt=brown-tail moth|1=Brown-tail moth}}. ==Toxicity== The {{ill|Seed|en|Seed|WD=Q40763|lt=Seed|1=Seed}}s are produced in pods similar to those of ''Laburnum'', and, like the seeds of that genus, are {{ill|poison|en|poison|WD=Q40867|lt=poison|1=Poison}}ous. All parts of the plant contain a {{ill|saponin|en|saponin|WD=Q207653|lt=saponin|1=Saponin}} called wisterin, which is {{ill|Toxicity|en|Toxicity|WD=Q274160|lt=toxic|1=Toxicity}} if ingested, and may cause {{ill|dizziness|en|dizziness|WD=Q10916362|lt=dizziness|1=Dizziness}}, confusion, speech problems, nausea, {{ill|Vomiting|en|Vomiting|WD=Q127076|lt=Vomiting|1=Vomiting}}, stomach pains, {{ill|Diarrhea|en|Diarrhea|WD=Q40878|lt=Diarrhea|1=Diarrhea}} and collapse. There is debate over whether the concentration outside of the seeds is sufficient to cause poisoning. Wisteria seeds have caused poisoning in children and pets of many countries, producing mild to severe gastroenteritis and other effects. ==Cultivation== {{multiple image |align=right |direction=horizontal |header_align=center |header= |image1=Wisteria at Nymans Gardens, West Sussex, England May 2006.JPG |width1=200 |alt1= |caption1=Wisteria at {{ill|Nymans|en|Nymans|WD=Q7071172|lt=Nymans|1=Nymans}} Gardens
({{ill|West Sussex|en|West Sussex|WD=Q23287|lt=West Sussex|1=West Sussex}}, England) |image2=Climbing_wisteria_(Stresa,_Italy).jpg |width2=200 |alt2= |caption2=Trunk of mature wisteria supported by balustrade ({{ill|Stresa|en|Stresa|WD=Q23700|lt=Stresa|1=Stresa}}, Italy) }} In North America, ''{{ill|Wisteria floribunda|en|Wisteria floribunda|WD=Q1329209|lt=W. floribunda|1=Wisteria floribunda}}'' (Japanese wisteria) and ''{{ill|Wisteria sinensis|en|Wisteria sinensis|WD=Q159116|lt=W. sinensis|1=Wisteria sinensis}}'' (Chinese wisteria) are far more popular than other species for their abundance of flowers, clusters of large flowers, variety of flower colors, and fragrance. ''W. sinensis'' was brought to the United States for horticultural purposes in 1816, while ''W. floribunda'' was introduced around 1830. Because of their hardiness and tendency to {{ill|escaped plant|en|escaped plant|WD=Q1494641|lt=escape cultivation|1=Escaped plant}}, these non-native wisterias are considered {{ill|Invasive species|en|Invasive species|WD=Q183368|lt=Invasive species|1=Invasive species}} in many parts of the {{ill|United States|en|United States|WD=Q30|lt=U.S.|1=United States}}, especially the {{ill|Southeastern United States|en|Southeastern United States|WD=Q1139046|lt=Southeast|1=Southeastern United States}}, due to their ability to overtake and choke out other native plant species. ''{{ill|Wisteria floribunda|en|Wisteria floribunda|WD=Q1329209|lt=W. floribunda|1=Wisteria floribunda}}'' (Japanese wisteria), which has the longest racemes of wisteria species, is decorative and has given rise to many {{ill|Cultivar|en|Cultivar|WD=Q4886|lt=Cultivar|1=Cultivar}}s that have won the prestigious {{ill|Award of Garden Merit|en|Award of Garden Merit|WD=Q3501416|lt=Award of Garden Merit|1=Award of Garden Merit}}. Wisteria, especially ''{{ill|Wisteria sinensis|en|Wisteria sinensis|WD=Q159116|lt=W. sinensis|1=Wisteria sinensis}}'' (Chinese wisteria), is very hardy and fast-growing. It can grow in fairly poor-quality soils, but prefers fertile, moist, well-drained soil. It thrives in full sun. It can be propagated via hardwood cutting, softwood cuttings, or seed. However, specimens grown from seed can take decades to bloom; for this reason, gardeners usually grow plants that have been started from rooted cuttings or grafted {{ill|Cultivar|en|Cultivar|WD=Q4886|lt=Cultivar|1=Cultivar}}s known to flower well. Another reason for failure to bloom can be excessive fertilizer (particularly {{ill|nitrogen|en|nitrogen|WD=Q627|lt=nitrogen|1=Nitrogen}}). Wisteria has nitrogen fixing capability (provided by ''{{ill|Rhizobia|en|Rhizobia|WD=Q9164450|lt=Rhizobia|1=Rhizobia}}'' bacteria in root nodules), and thus mature plants may benefit from added {{ill|potassium|en|potassium|WD=Q703|lt=potassium|1=Potassium}} and {{ill|phosphate|en|phosphate|WD=Q46220103|lt=phosphate|1=Phosphate}}, but not nitrogen. Finally, wisteria can be reluctant to bloom before it has reached maturity. Maturation may require only a few years, as in ''{{ill|Wisteria macrostachya|en|Wisteria macrostachya|WD=Q8027752|lt=W. macrostachya|1=Wisteria macrostachya}}'' (Kentucky wisteria), or nearly twenty, as in ''W. sinensis''. Maturation can be forced by physically abusing the main {{ill|Trunk (botany)|en|Trunk (botany)|WD=Q193472|lt=trunk|1=Trunk (botany)}}, root pruning, or {{ill|Drought|en|Drought|WD=Q43059|lt=Drought|1=Drought}} stress. Wisteria can grow into a mound when unsupported, but is at its best when allowed to clamber up a tree, {{ill|pergola|en|pergola|WD=Q264458|lt=pergola|1=Pergola}}, wall, or other supporting structure. ''W. floribunda'' (Japanese wisteria) with longer racemes is the best choice to grow along a pergola. ''W. sinensis'' (Chinese wisteria) with shorter racemes is the best choice for growing along a wall. Whatever the case, the support must be very sturdy, because mature wisteria can become immensely strong with heavy wrist-thick {{ill|Trunk (botany)|en|Trunk (botany)|WD=Q193472|lt=trunk|1=Trunk (botany)}}s and {{ill|Plant stem|en|Plant stem|WD=Q134267|lt=stem|1=Plant stem}}s. These can collapse latticework, crush thin wooden posts, and even strangle large trees. Wisteria allowed to grow on houses can cause damage to gutters, downspouts, and similar structures. Wisteria flowers develop in buds near the base of the previous year's growth, so {{ill|pruning|en|pruning|WD=Q500094|lt=pruning|1=Pruning}} back side shoots to the basal few buds in early spring can enhance the visibility of the flowers. If it is desired to control the size of the plant, the side shoots can be shortened to between 20 and 40 cm long in midsummer, and back to {{convert|10|to|20|cm}} in the fall. Once the plant is a few years old, a relatively compact, free-flowering form can be achieved by pruning off the new tendrils three times during the growing season in the summer months. The flowers of some varieties are edible, and can even be used to make wine. Others are said to be toxic. Careful identification by an expert is strongly recommended before consuming this or any wild plant. In the United Kingdom, the national collection of wisteria is held by Chris Lane at the Witch Hazel Nursery in {{ill|Newington, Swale|en|Newington, Swale|WD=Q10748183|lt=Newington|1=Newington, Swale}}, near {{ill|Sittingbourne|en|Sittingbourne|WD=Q1626044|lt=Sittingbourne|1=Sittingbourne}} in {{ill|Kent|en|Kent|WD=Q23298|lt=Kent|1=Kent}}. {{Clear}} ==Art and symbolism== [[File:Sagari Fuji (No background and Black color drawing).svg|thumb|right|150px|{{transliteration|ja|Sagari fuji mon}} (Wisteria {{transliteration|ja|[[Mon (emblem)|mon]]}})]] Wisteria and their racemes have been widely used in Japan throughout the centuries and were a popular symbol in {{nihongo3|family crests||[[Mon (emblem)|mon]]}} and heraldry. Wisteria is one of the five most commonly used motifs in the {{transliteration|ja|mon}}, and there are more than 150 types of wisteria {{transliteration|ja|mon}}. Because of its longevity and fertility, wisteria was considered an auspicious plant and was favored as a {{transliteration|ja|mon}}, and was adopted and popularized by the [[Fujiwara clan]] as their {{transliteration|ja|mon}}.{{cite web|url=https://www.nippon.com/en/japan-data/h01578/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230420034414/https://www.nippon.com/en/japan-data/h01578/|title="Kamon": Japan's Family Crests|publisher=nippon.com|date=10 February 2023|archive-date=20 April 2023|access-date=29 April 2023}}{{cite web|url=https://irohakamon.com/kamon/fuji/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230212111436/https://irohakamon.com/kamon/fuji/|script-title=ja:藤紋（ふじ）について|language=ja|publisher=Kamon no iroha|archive-date=12 February 2023|access-date=29 April 2023}} {{multiple image |direction=horizontal |width1=147 |width2=150 |align=left |footer=Left to right: ''View of Oyster Bay'' (1908), by [[:en:Louis C. Tiffany|Louis C. Tiffany]], with wisteria evoking the estate of its patrons, {{ill|Wistariahurst|en|Wistariahurst|WD=Q8027742|lt=Wistariahurst|1=Wistariahurst}}; ''Japanese wisteria and white-bellied green pigeons'' (1883), a woodblock print by {{ill|Kōno Bairei|en|Kōno Bairei|WD=Q3201302|lt=Kōno Bairei|1=Kōno Bairei}} |image1=At the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York 2017 04 - View of Oyster Bay. New York City.jpg |image2=Bairei kachō gafu, Spring 12, Japanese wisteria and white-bellied green pigeons.jpg}} One popular dance in {{ill|Kabuki|en|Kabuki|WD=Q199701|lt=Kabuki|1=Kabuki}} known as the ''{{ill|Fuji Musume|en|Fuji Musume|WD=Q11623783|lt=Fuji Musume|1=Fuji Musume}}'' (or 'The Wisteria Maiden'), is the sole extant dance of a series of five personifying dances in which a maiden becomes the embodiment of the spirit of wisteria. In the West, both in building materials such as tile, as well as stained glass, wisterias have been used both in realism and stylistically in artistic works and industrial design. {{Clear}} ==References== {{Reflist|refs= {{cite book |last=Baird |first=Merrily C. |year=2001 |title=Symbols of Japan: Thematic Motifs in Art and Design |publisher=Random House, Inc. |location=New York |page=67 |oclc=237418692}} {{cite book |last=Bryson |first=Bill |author-link=Bill Bryson |title=A Short History of Nearly Everything |edition=1st |year=2003 |publisher=Broadway Books |location=New York, NY |isbn=0-375-43200-0 |chapter=Ch. 6 — Science Red in Tooth and Claw |url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780375432002}} {{cite web |last=Charters |first=Michael L. |work=California Plant Names: Latin and Greek Meanings and Derivations |title=Page W |url=http://www.calflora.net/botanicalnames/pageW.html |access-date=2011-05-15}} {{Cite journal |last1=Compton |first1=James A. |last2=Schrire |first2=Brian D. |last3=Könyves |first3=Kálmán |last4=Forest |first4=Félix |last5=Malakasi |first5=Panagiota |last6=Sawai Mattapha |last7=Sirichamorn |first7=Yotsawate |date=2019 |title=The ''Callerya'' Group redefined and Tribe Wisterieae (Fabaceae) emended based on morphology and data from nuclear and chloroplast DNA sequences |journal=PhytoKeys |issue=125 |pages=1–112 |doi=10.3897/phytokeys.125.34877 |pmid=31303810 |pmc=6610001 |name-list-style=amp |doi-access=free }} {{cite book |last1=Cotter |first1=John L. |last2=Roberts |first2=Daniel G. |last3=Parrington |first3=Michael |year=1994 |title=The Buried Past: An Archaeological History of Philadelphia |publication-place=Philadelphia |publisher=University of Pennsylvania Press |page=339 |name-list-style=amp}} {{Cite web |date=15 April 2014 |title=Canadian Poisonous Plants Information System -
